title: Unsure about God, and still here
hookLine: can you be Jewish and unsure about God? a midrash imagines God answering

lines: AN ANSWER IN AN OLD BOOK.
cards: It isn't about food or holidays. It's this: can I be Jewish if I'm not sure I believe in God? Some people carry that question quietly for years.
Some decide the answer must be no, and stay away from everything, the candles, the seder, the synagogue, because they feel like a fraud.
Today, the biggest question of all, and an answer the rabbis tucked into an old book about grief.

teach.h: IF ONLY THEY KEPT MY TORAH.
teach.b: The rabbis tell it as if God were speaking.
In a midrash on the book of Lamentations, God says, more or less: if only they had left Me, and kept My Torah, because the light inside it would bring them back. Read that again.
In the tradition's own imagination, God is less worried about whether people believe than about whether they keep learning and doing. Keep the Torah, and the light inside it will do its own work.
In Hebrew, hamaor shebah: the light that's in it. It fits a pattern you've met before.

teach.h: WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.
teach.b: At Sinai, on day ten, the people said we will do, and we will hear. Doing came first. Judaism has long been a people and a practice, not only a set of beliefs.
Some Jews light candles, sit at the seder and argue over the Talmud while unsure about God. Others are sure. They sit at the same table.
Traditions differ here, and it's worth saying how. Maimonides wrote thirteen principles of faith, beginning with belief in God, and in much of Orthodox teaching belief stands at the center.
Other teachers and movements put people, practice and questions first, and Humanistic Judaism builds Jewish life without centering God at all. This path won't rank them.

What a week of study adds is this: the house of study has always been full of questions, asked out loud, in pairs, across a table. A question about God is still a question about God. You can bring it in with you.

how: Jewish communities hold a wide range of views on belief: many Orthodox Jews hold Maimonides' principles of faith as central, while many other Jews take part in study, holidays and community life while still questioning, and some movements put practice and peoplehood first.

o: the light in Torah study that brings people back
the light of the menorah that burned in the Temple
the glow said to shine on Moses' face after Sinai

games.q: what's inside today — tap the pairs.
p: we will do, and we will hear

s: you have to settle what you believe before you can take part
the midrash pictures learning and doing bringing their own light.
every Jewish movement treats belief the same way
much Orthodox teaching centers Maimonides' principles; other movements put people and practice first.
at Sinai, doing came before understanding
the people said: we will do, and we will hear.

games.q: a friend says: i light candles every Friday, but i'm not sure about God. am i a fraud?
o: yes: belief has to come first.
not in the midrash's picture: the doing carries its own light.
games.why: the midrash imagines God saying: keep my Torah, and the light inside it will bring them back. traditions differ on how central belief is, and this path doesn't rank them.

practice: Whatever you believe about God today, or don't, let it be exactly what it is, and don't argue with it.
Picture a study table, two people, an open book, two cups of coffee going cold, and set your question down on it like a book you brought along: not to solve it, just to have it in the room.
If you pray, you can pray with the question; if not, let the question keep you company.

wordCard.voice: Hamaor shebah. The light that's in it: the midrash's idea that the learning and the doing carry their own light.

orig.note: Hebrew: the light that is in it, from the rabbis' teaching on Lamentations.

carryVoice: Your line: the light inside it. You can start with the learning and the doing, and let the questions come along. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
